newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Crude Outlook - Quiet, but eye on futures.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook - Quiet, but eye on futures.

text.p: A slump in global futures prices is unlikely to have any immediate impact on Asian wet crude markets which will not start trading for some days yet, traders said.

This week is expected to be quiet while the Chinese market remains closed for the Lunar New Year, but premiums are seen weakening for April from March trading anyhow amid a seasonal fall in demand, traders said.
April trading could pick up late this week and get into full swing next week, when swing-buyer China comes back to the market, they said.

"Traders will keep a low profile for a while because they are reluctant to get into serious talks before knowing for sure what China's buying interest is like after the long holiday," one trader said.
But global futures have slumped during the Lunar New Year holiday break, which started on Friday and included Monday.
Front-month Brent dropped almost $2.00 per barrel over the weekend. On Tuesday on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange it was quoted at $21.08/$21.16 from $22.47 on Thursday.
The fall was partly technical, with Brent giving up some support levels, while the NYMEX complex was weak at the same time with seasonal demand on heating oil dropping away.
For Asia, demand for March cargoes was said to have been mostly satisfied, while one Dubai, partial Murban, and possibly one Oman cargo were still available for March-lifting.

Traders said Japanese and South Korean requirements for April cargoes were likely to be substantially smaller than those for March as several refineries in the countries are scheduled to be shut down for routine maintenance in April and May.
Japan demand for crude in April is expected to slacken also because of ample oil product stocks, especially middle distillates, which would hit the lighter MidEast grades.
Japan's kerosene stocks were up 33 percent at the end of 1996 from 1995, gas oil was up 44 percent and heavy fuel oil 10 percent.
Some traders expected initial premiums for April Oman to be in the single digits amid bearish sentiment for April barrels.
March Oman initially traded at about MPM plus 30 cents, but later slumped to around 10 cents and held that level to the end of March trading.

Among light Middle Eastern crudes, Qatar Land premiums were seen under pressure after the price differential between Qatar Land and Dubai widened eight cents covering January OSPs, despite general expectations of a weak market for April. The Oman differential also widened against Dubai to $1.14 from $1.04, while ADNOC grades came in three to four cents.

In regional grades, traders said Minas crude is likely to kick off March trading at around ICP plus 70 cents. February Minas was mostly traded above ICP plus $1.00, but late deals have dropped to 75 cents.
In term price talks for Bach Ho crude oil, traders said Vietnam and Japanese trading houses were near accord.
Vietnam's offer price was at about APPI Minas quotes plus 85 cents for a six-month period starting in April, compared with the current term premium of 63 cents, traders said.
The Japanese trading houses were said to be bidding with the premium of around 80 cents.
